title: Mirabai's devotion
hookLine: Hindu bhakti poets like Mirabai loved Krishna with their whole lives

cards: A woman of a royal household walks out of the palace to sing in the temple with wandering holy men. She dances in front of an image of Krishna.
Her in-laws are mortified: a woman of her rank should stay behind the walls, not sing in the street with strangers. She keeps singing anyway.
Her name, as the stories give it, is Mirabai, and the songs said to be hers are still sung in homes and temples. Today's word is the thing she gave her whole life to.

teach.b: Bhakti is Sanskrit, usually translated devotion: a loving, personal turning toward God.

The Bhagavad Gita uses it, where Krishna speaks of those who worship him with bhakti, and it names whole movements of poet-saints who sang their love for God in everyday languages. Mirabai is one of them.
Much of her story comes from legend, and the details vary. In the stories, she gives her heart to Krishna as a child and later calls him her true husband. Her new family tries to stop her devotion.
Tradition says they even sent her poison, and she drank it as an offering, and it did her no harm.
Her songs speak to Krishna directly, as someone near. One refrain, in paraphrase: mine is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no one else.
They're plain and intimate, full of waiting, teasing, longing and joy, meant to be sung, not studied. For bhakti poets, devotion isn't a feeling saved for a holy day.
It reorganizes everything: where you go, whom you sit with, what you sing while you work.

Some Hindus practice bhakti through temple worship and festivals, others by chanting a name of God through the day. Mirabai's story shows what that love can cost, and, in the stories, she paid it singing.

how: Hindus practice bhakti in many ways, among them temple worship, festivals, and singing devotional songs (bhajans and kirtan), and songs attributed to Mirabai are still sung in homes and temples.

games.why: in the stories she keeps singing, even when tradition says they sent her poison.

practice: Bhakti is often sung, so this practice uses your voice: think of someone or something you love deeply and hum for them, quietly, any tune or none.
Let the hum say thank you, or I miss you, or I'm glad you exist, and if it feels strange, hum softly anyway and notice where it vibrates in your chest.
If you pray, a devotional song or name from your own tradition can take the place of the hum.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Sanskrit for loving devotion to God, the path of the poet-saints like Mirabai, who sang it with her whole life. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: devotion, loving worship of God; the word the Bhagavad Gita uses.
